chunks: "The big danger is thermal runaway. A lithium cell has a flammable organic electrolyte and a lot of stored energy in a sealed package.
If something pushes it outside its safe window, like overcharge, overdischarge, a short circuit, a crush or puncture, or just excessive heat, it starts to heat up internally.
Heat speeds up the reactions that produce more heat, and above roughly 100 to 150 degrees C it becomes self-sustaining.
The cell vents flammable gas, can catch fire, and can set off the cells next to it. Fumes can also be toxic, because the electrolyte salt can form hydrogen fluoride.
Also, a short on a big pack is an electrical hazard with hundreds of amps of arc and burns. Prevention is layered.
At the cell level you have a separator that shuts down, a vent, and sometimes a current-interrupt device.
At the pack level you have a protector or BMS with over-voltage, under-voltage, over-current, short-circuit and temperature cutoffs, plus a fuse.
The charger enforces CC/CV with a temperature check and a timer. Mechanically you protect the cell from crush and puncture and leave room for swelling.
And you pick the chemistry: LiFePO4 is much more tolerant than cobalt-based cells. Finally there's handling: charging unattended, storage and transport rules."
